newsitem.title: USA: Houston says $500 mln bond needs no new taxes.
newsitem.headline: Houston says $500 mln bond needs no new taxes.

text.p: Houston's proposed $500 million general obligation bond, due to go to a referendum in November, can be financed without raising property or other taxes, the director of the city's finance administration said.
Richard Lewis said Houston's revenue growth has climbed at a steady four percent per year in the past five years and should continue at a similar pace in the years ahead.
"So I think we can authorize this without raising taxes," Lewis told Reuters in a telephone interview on Monday.
"Also, our revenue reserves (total revenues minus debt service payments) have gone up dramatically to over seven percent (of total revenues) from 3.5 percent in the past," he said.
Houston currently has a property tax of 66.5 cents per $100 of valuation, and has no garbage collection fee.
The bond program, which must be authorized by the City Council before being placed on the November ballot, covers five years of public works beginning next year.
Lewis said each year's addition of new debt should be offset by the retirement of existing debts.
The city's total outstanding bonded debt at the end of April was $4.7 billion, of which $1.5 billion was in general obligation bonds.

Lewis said about 40 percent of the planned debt issue will go for street reconstruction with the rest set aside for drainage systems, upgrading branch libraries and fire stations and for parks and recreation facilities.
Houston voters last year rejected a school bond proposal for a similar amount, but Lewis said he was confident the city would win approval for the general obligation bond.
"I think the people of Houston realize the city is in good financial shape and would want that to continue into the next century," he said.
Harris County, where Houston is located, is also considering a $370 million road construction bond program but Lewis said he did not think that would affect Houston's plans.
He said the city, which accounts for 57 percent of Harris County's tax base, is working with county officials to see that Houston gets its fair share of any new road investment.
Alex Fraser, a Dallas-based analyst with Standard & Poor's, said he does not expect Houston's bond program to cause any major change in its debt structure.

"It is a large program but they have done similar ones before. So we are not concerned and I don't expect any change in the rating," he said. Houston currently has a Double A Minus rating from Standard & Poor's.
